title: Canary rollouts: upgrade models in production without downtime
gist: Together AI details a production rollout system (canary, blue-green, rolling) that moves LLM inference traffic between model checkpoints with automated capacity/health/metric gates, and demonstrates it live by catching a 137% p95 latency regression when canarying Qwen2.5-7B to Qwen3.5-9B and reversing it with zero failed requests across 6,800 probe requests.

insights.claim: Together AI frames its rollout feature as replacing human-in-the-loop safety (a person watching dashboards and manually shifting traffic) with a platform-enforced staged migration, contrasting it against a 'hard swap' (all traffic moved at once, failures discovered via dashboard or customers) and a 'DIY staged cutover' (a second deployment plus a manual script nudging traffic while watching Grafana).
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Signals Together AI is competing on operational/MLOps maturity, not just model access or raw inference price -- a differentiator versus inference platforms that only offer swap-the-endpoint deployment.
insights.quote: Both of these options put a human in the loop as the safety mechanism. Rollouts move that mechanism into the platform: you describe the source, the target, the steps, and what "healthy" means, and the platform works against this plan at every stage.

insights.claim: Together AI offers three rollout strategies on the same endpoint: canary (traffic moves in staged percentages, default ladder 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%, with wait periods and optional metric gates), blue-green (a single gated 0% -> 100% cutover, described as a one-step canary), and rolling (an in-place, replica-by-replica swap that preserves total capacity, best for capacity-constrained or same-model config changes).
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A menu of rollout strategies tailored to different constraints (capacity, speed, risk tolerance) suggests the feature targets serious production/enterprise inference customers, not hobbyist API users.

insights.claim: Every canary step follows a fixed sequence designed to prevent specific incident classes: the target scales up before any traffic moves, the health gate runs before traffic shifts, a propagation wait sits between the shift and the source drain (so routing caches converge), the source drains only after traffic has moved, and the wait/metric gate must pass before a step is recorded complete.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: The deliberate step ordering is an engineering moat argument: it's the kind of operational detail that is easy to get wrong and costly to discover in production, so a working implementation is a credible signal of platform engineering depth.
insights.quote: Capacity leads traffic on the way up; traffic leads capacity on the way down.
insights.locator: Here's what happens inside every canary step

insights.claim: The platform makes six explicit guarantees across all three rollout strategies: capacity is never rounded down; traffic never lands on capacity that isn't ready; each side always keeps the replicas its current traffic share needs (or the rollout pauses as UNDER_SERVED); the rollout only raises replica floors rather than overriding autoscaler maximums (or pauses as POLICY_INFEASIBLE); every gate always returns a definitive verdict; and gates require minimum sample sizes (p95 needs 20 requests in the window, p99 needs 100) or pause as METRICS_UNAVAILABLE.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: These are SLA-grade guarantees (not just best-effort scripting) -- the kind of formal reliability contract enterprise buyers evaluate when choosing an inference platform for production LLM workloads.
insights.quote: p95 needs 20 requests in the window and p99 needs 100; with fewer the rollout pauses as METRICS_UNAVAILABLE.

insights.claim: Metric gates (staged latency/error/load comparisons) are exclusive to the canary strategy -- blue-green and rolling still run basic health gates but skip the staged metric comparison because it requires canary's multi-step structure to be meaningful.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Positions canary as the only strategy suited for validating a risky model swap on live traffic before full cutover -- a concrete reason enterprise ML teams might choose Together AI's canary over a faster but less-monitored blue-green swap elsewhere.
insights.quote: Metric gates are a canary feature: blue-green and rolling still run health gates, but the staged metric comparison needs canary's step structure to be meaningful.
insights.locator: Under the hood: configuring the gates

insights.claim: The platform supports two gate check types: a relative regressionCheck (target must not be more than N% worse than source, recommended default for latency because it self-calibrates without needing a known absolute p95) and an absolute thresholdCheck (target must satisfy a hard operator/value bound, recommended when there's a fixed SLO or the source itself might already be unhealthy).
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A dual gate design (relative + absolute) shows the product anticipates real operational nuance (e.g., an already-degraded source), which reduces false-positive/false-negative risk for customers relying on automated gating.
insights.quote: regressionCheck (relative): "the target must not be more than N% worse than the source." This is the right default for latency, because it self-calibrates

insights.claim: Gate timing is mechanically constrained: the wait period must be at least the metric window plus roughly 90 seconds of ingestion lag, and the platform auto-extends an under-sized wait; with the default 5-minute window, the default 3-minute step interval is automatically grown to 390 seconds (6m30s).
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Quantifies the real time-cost of safe canarying (~6.5 minutes per gated step minimum) versus blue-green's ~30-second propagation wait -- a concrete latency-vs-safety tradeoff customers must budget for when planning model upgrades.
insights.quote: a 5m window needs a 6.5m wait period. With the default 5m window the platform grows the default 3m interval to 390s (6m 30s)

insights.claim: By design there is no automatic rollback on a regression: a tripped gate always routes to SYSTEM_PAUSED for human review, because moving traffic back is itself considered a change that should be watched; only recoverable failure causes (capacity shortfall, metrics-pipeline gap) are auto-retried, every 15 minutes for up to 3 hours, before the platform leaves it paused for a human.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A deliberate 'no silent auto-rollback' design choice reflects a conservative, human-in-the-loop philosophy for production changes -- relevant to how risk-averse enterprise buyers will perceive Together AI's reliability posture versus more 'fully automated' competitors.
insights.quote: There is no automatic abort: a confirmed regression always parks the rollout for a human, because moving traffic back is itself a change someone should be watching.

themes.theme: Live demo: quantified regression catch (Qwen2.5-7B to Qwen3.5-9B)

insights.claim: In a live September 2026 demo upgrading a production endpoint from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3.5-9B-FP8 (each on a single H100, under a steady 5 requests/second of chat completions), a canary gate with a 25% p95 latency regression budget tripped at the 10% traffic step: the target's p95 router latency measured 1,740 ms versus 734 ms on the source, a 137% regression.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A concrete, reproducible worked example (not just marketing copy) gives investors and technical buyers verifiable evidence the feature works on real production traffic, which matters for due diligence on Together AI's platform claims.
insights.quote: The 9B's p95 router latency was 1,740 ms against 734 ms on the 7B, a 137% regression against the 25% budget.

insights.claim: The team attributed the latency regression to model behavior rather than a platform bug: Qwen3.5-9B is a reasoning model that generates more tokens per request at the same max_tokens setting than Qwen2.5-7B, making it a product decision to cancel the rollout rather than something to simply resume past.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Illustrates a broader industry pattern: newer 'reasoning' models can regress latency/cost metrics even when eval quality improves, which is a recurring operational risk for anyone upgrading production LLM deployments industry-wide, not just on Together AI.
insights.quote: the 9B is a reasoning model and, at the same max_tokens, generates more per request. That is a product decision rather than something to resume past

insights.claim: After canceling the tripped canary, the traffic split froze at 90%/10% within 0.2 seconds; a subsequent reverse blue-green rollout fully restored 100% of traffic to the original Qwen2.5-7B deployment in 5 minutes 49 seconds; across the entire exercise (traffic shift, pause, cancel, and reverse) the probe logged 6,800 requests with 0 non-200 responses.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Zero failed requests through a real regression-and-recovery cycle is the core value proposition made concrete -- the kind of metric an enterprise customer would cite when justifying migrating production inference workloads to Together AI.
insights.quote: The probe's verdict across the whole run, including the shift, the pause, the cancel and the reverse: 6,800 requests, 0 non-200 responses.

insights.claim: A separate, earlier test run in July 2026 using a deliberately impossible threshold gate produced the same outcome shape -- a trip at 10% of traffic -- and logged 1,198 probe requests with zero errors through the full recovery, suggesting the pause/cancel/reverse mechanism is reproducible rather than a one-off cherry-picked demo.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A repeat clean result across two separate test runs months apart strengthens confidence the zero-downtime claim is a real platform property rather than a lucky single run, relevant for technical due diligence.
insights.quote: An earlier run in July, with a deliberately impossible threshold gate, produced the same shape: a trip at 10% of traffic and 1,198 probe requests with zero errors through the recovery.
insights.locator: Final paragraph before Try it yourself

insights.claim: Rollouts expose four controls (pause, resume, promote, cancel) but deliberately have no 'rollback' verb; reversing a rollout requires creating an entirely new rollout with source and target swapped, and after a cancel, the default canary ladder automatically skips steps the new target has already passed.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: The 'reverse is just another forward rollout' design keeps the safety gates active even during a revert, avoiding a common failure mode where 'emergency rollback' code paths bypass normal safety checks.
insights.quote: There is no rollback verb. To move traffic back, after a cancel or after a completion, create a new rollout with source and target swapped, then start it.

insights.claim: Canceling a rollout does not scale anything down; it freezes the current traffic split as the endpoint's new standing weights, and both deployments continue serving their frozen shares (consuming GPU capacity) until an operator explicitly edits the split, deletes the target, or runs a reverse rollout.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A frozen-but-not-cleaned-up cancel state means customers can accrue extra GPU cost (paying for both old and new deployments) if they don't actively clean up after a canceled rollout -- a real operational/cost detail for anyone modeling Together AI's or a customer's GPU spend.
insights.quote: A target canceled at 0% is left running with no traffic; scale it to zero or delete it if you no longer need it.

insights.claim: Promote (skip to 100%) is not instantaneous even though it skips the intermediate canary steps: in a test run with a 10-minute step interval, a promote issued at step 0 still had to sit through the final step's full soak/wait period before completing.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Shows the safety gates are not bypassable for operator convenience -- even a manual 'go faster' command still respects the minimum soak time, reinforcing that the platform prioritizes safety guarantees over pure speed.
insights.quote: Not instantaneous: in a test run with a 10-minute step interval, a promote at step 0 still sat through the final step's full soak.

insights.claim: Pause is a first-class persistent state, not a held connection, and is designed to survive multi-day pauses and resume exactly where it left off; the platform never auto-resumes an operator-initiated pause.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Multi-day pause support without babysitting lowers the operational burden of doing careful staged rollouts, making the safety features practical to actually use rather than a feature customers avoid due to overhead.
insights.quote: Pause is not a held connection but rather a first-class state. Rollouts are designed to survive multi-day pauses and resume exactly where they left off.
insights.locator: Edge cases, Can I pause indefinitely?

insights.claim: The rollout API and CLI (tg, shipped in the together Python package v2.34.0+) are strict and typed: percentiles must be integers, enum values must carry full type prefixes (METRIC_STAT_TYPE_*, REGRESSION_DIRECTION_*, THRESHOLD_OPERATOR_*), durations are protobuf-style strings ('600s'), and requesting a metric name outside a closed catalog is rejected at creation time with a 400 error listing supported names.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Strict, well-typed API surfaces (versus loose scripting glue) signal a production-grade internal engine, supporting the case that Together AI is investing in durable platform/MLOps infrastructure rather than shipping thin wrappers around inference endpoints.
insights.quote: percentile is an integer (95, not "p95"), enum values carry their full prefix (METRIC_STAT_TYPE_*, REGRESSION_DIRECTION_*, THRESHOLD_OPERATOR_*), durations are protobuf strings like "600s"

insights.claim: Rollout failures are classified into typed, documented categories -- METRIC_REGRESSION, METRICS_UNAVAILABLE, CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED, UNDER_SERVED, and POLICY_INFEASIBLE -- each paired with an explicit recommended operator action, and the platform guards against false alarms by re-querying metrics data multiple times over ~90 seconds before pausing on a suspected regression.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Bharti, Zarni Phyo, Zain Hasan, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A typed failure taxonomy with prescribed remediation reads as an SRE-grade operational playbook baked directly into the product -- the kind of maturity that helps Together AI sell into enterprise teams with strict production SLAs, differentiating it from less operationally mature inference API providers.
insights.quote: before it pauses on a regression the system re-queries several times over ~90 seconds to make sure it isn't looking at ingestion lag or transient blips, and a gate that cannot get trustworthy data pauses with METRICS_UNAVAILABLE rather than counting as a regression
